title: Chapter 10 — Can the Computer Just Tell Us?
text:
A data scientist at the Tanzania Ministry of Health sits in front of ten years of monthly facility-level data — 60,000 rows, 40 columns. Her director walks in and says “just run an algorithm and tell us what’s causing what”. Modern algorithms can do remarkable things. But there is one thing they fundamentally cannot do — and the cannot is the most important lesson in the course.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: Data alone cannot tell you the direction of a causal arrow. Data plus a few expert assumptions can — and that is what structure learning really is.

title: Chapter 10 — Can the Computer Just Tell Us?
section: R workshop — run the PC algorithm, then run into the wall
text:
R workshop — run the PC algorithm, then run into the wall
In the lecture, Esther handed her data to a structure-learning algorithm and got back a network with mostly undirected edges. In this workshop you’ll do the same on a small simulated MNH dataset and watch the wall appear in your console.

Setting up

library(bnlearn)
library(dplyr)

set.seed(42)



Build a small simulated dataset
We’ll generate data from a known causal structure, then ask the algorithm to recover it. The known truth is:

RegionalBudget → Stockouts
RegionalBudget → StaffShortage
Stockouts → MaternalDeaths
StaffShortage → MaternalDeaths


n <- 1000

regional_budget <- sample(c("low", "high"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.5, 0.5))

stockouts <- ifelse(regional_budget == "low",
                    sample(c("yes", "no"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3)),
                    sample(c("yes", "no"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.8)))

staff_shortage <- ifelse(regional_budget == "low",
                         sample(c("yes", "no"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
                         sample(c("yes", "no"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.8)))

maternal_deaths <- ifelse(stockouts == "yes" | staff_shortage == "yes",
                          sample(c("high", "low"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)),
                          sample(c("high", "low"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.15, 0.85)))

dhis_data <- data.frame(
  RegionalBudget  = factor(regional_budget),
  Stockouts       = factor(stockouts),
  StaffShortage   = factor(staff_shortage),
  MaternalDeaths  = factor(maternal_deaths)
)

head(dhis_data)



Run the PC algorithm

# The PC algorithm — Spirtes-Glymour-Scheines (2000), the foundational
# structure-learning algorithm.
learned_network <- pc.stable(dhis_data)

learned_network



Look at the discovered structure

plot(learned_network)

# What edges did the algorithm find?
arcs(learned_network)

# Which of those edges are DIRECTED, and which are still undirected?
directed.arcs(learned_network)
undirected.arcs(learned_network)

What you should see: the algorithm found roughly the right connectivity — it identified that RegionalBudget is linked to both Stockouts and StaffShortage, and that both of those are linked to MaternalDeaths. But many of the edges came back undirected. That’s the wall from the lecture.
Even though we built the data from a clear causal structure, the algorithm could not always recover the directions from the data alone — because multiple causal stories produce the same conditional-independence pattern.


Now hand the algorithm an expert hint

# Esther tells the algorithm: "I'm absolutely certain that RegionalBudget
# is upstream of everything else — it's a budget cycle, it can't be
# caused by stockouts." That's a domain assumption the algorithm cannot
# discover on its own.
blacklist <- data.frame(
  from = c("Stockouts", "StaffShortage", "MaternalDeaths",
           "Stockouts", "StaffShortage", "MaternalDeaths"),
  to   = c("RegionalBudget", "RegionalBudget", "RegionalBudget",
           "RegionalBudget", "RegionalBudget", "RegionalBudget")
)

learned_with_expert <- pc.stable(dhis_data, blacklist = blacklist)

plot(learned_with_expert)
arcs(learned_with_expert)

What you should see: with the single domain hint “nothing causes RegionalBudget”, more edges become directed. The algorithm could not discover this on its own, but once an expert gives it the orientation, the rest of the picture falls into place.
That is the loop the lecture describes. Algorithm + expert > algorithm alone > expert alone.

You run a structure-learning algorithm on a Kenyan county dataset. It finds a strong undirected edge between facility births and newborn deaths. What are at least three different stories the data could be telling? Hint: review chains, forks, colliders, and hidden variables — and don’t forget the most dangerous explanation: that the algorithm picked up a reporting artefact, not a real causal link.

title: Chapter 8 — Spreading the Money
text:
A programme officer has a fixed MNH budget and four countries. Her board meets in three weeks and wants one slide. Concentrate? Spread? Tier? Each strategy has a different shape of risk — and the average expected value alone cannot pick a winner.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: Spreading resources is not a math question — it’s a question about which uncertainties you’re willing to live with. The expected value picks a centre. The shape of the range picks a strategy.

section: R workshop — Monte Carlo Grace’s three strategies
text:
R workshop — Monte Carlo Grace’s three strategies
In the lecture, Grace compared concentrate, spread, and tier on expected value alone — and saw that the expected values didn’t pick a winner. In this workshop you’ll run a Monte Carlo simulation for each strategy in R and see the shapes of the three histograms directly.

Setting up

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

set.seed(42)  # so the random draws are reproducible



The four countries

# Per-quarter-budget estimates from the lecture table.
# Each country has a "low" and "high" estimate; we treat the truth as
# uniformly distributed between them — a rough but defensible assumption.
countries <- tibble::tribble(
  ~country,    ~low,  ~high,
  "Ethiopia",   600,  1800,
  "Rwanda",     700,  1100,
  "Kenya",      400,  1600,
  "Tanzania",   500,  1700
)

countries



Simulate one possible future

# For one possible future, draw one outcome per country.
# (Quarter-budget effect — we'll scale by allocation share below.)
draw_one_future <- function() {
  countries |>
    mutate(outcome = runif(n(), low, high))
}

draw_one_future()



Run 10,000 futures for each strategy

# Concentrate: all the money on Ethiopia (highest expected value).
# Scale-up factor of 4 with diminishing returns: a 4x budget gets you ~3x outcome.
concentrate_strategy <- function() {
  draw <- runif(1, 600, 1800)  # Ethiopia draw
  draw * 3                       # diminishing-returns scale-up
}

# Spread: each country gets one quarter — sum the four outcomes.
spread_strategy <- function() {
  futures <- draw_one_future()
  sum(futures$outcome)
}

# Tier: 40% Ethiopia, 40% Tanzania (top two), 10% Rwanda, 10% Kenya.
tier_strategy <- function() {
  futures <- draw_one_future()
  weights <- c(Ethiopia = 1.6, Rwanda = 0.4, Kenya = 0.4, Tanzania = 1.6)
  sum(futures$outcome * weights[futures$country])
}

# Run each strategy 10,000 times.
n_sims <- 10000
sims <- tibble(
  Concentrate = replicate(n_sims, concentrate_strategy()),
  Spread      = replicate(n_sims, spread_strategy()),
  Tier        = replicate(n_sims, tier_strategy())
)

summary(sims)



Compare the three histograms

sims_long <- sims |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "strategy", values_to = "lives_saved")

ggplot(sims_long, aes(x = lives_saved, fill = strategy)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 50) +
  facet_wrap(~strategy, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Three strategies, three risk shapes",
    subtitle = "Each histogram is 10,000 simulated futures",
    x        = "Lives saved",
    y        = "Number of futures"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

What you should see:

Concentrate — a wide histogram with a long left tail. Best case is huge; worst case is the worst of any strategy.
Spread — a fat blob in the middle. Almost no futures are great; almost no futures are terrible.
Tier — a narrower bell shifted right of spread, with a higher floor than concentrate.

This is the conversation Grace needs to have with her board — not “whose number is bigger” but “which shape of risk are we willing to live with”.


Answer the board’s real question

# What fraction of futures end up under 3000 lives saved?
sims_long |>
  group_by(strategy) |>
  summarise(
    pct_under_3000 = mean(lives_saved < 3000)
  )

That’s the number that decides the board meeting. “There is a 12% chance of ending up under 3000 lives saved” is a sentence a board member can argue with. “The expected value is 4500” is not.

text:
Try it yourself
You have a fixed MNH budget. Three options: (A) a national rollout in a country with strong recent results but moderate uncertainty; (B) a regional pilot in a country with weak recent results but very high upside if it works; (C) a 50/50 split. Sketch the three risk shapes without computing anything. Which one would you bring to the board, and why?

title: Chapter 6 — When the Data Lies in Two Directions
text:
A Kenyan voucher programme looks like a 10-percentage-point success in the aggregate. Split by access to a clinic, the relationship reverses — the voucher does worse than no voucher in every access group. Same data. Opposite story. Which version should you trust?






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: When data tells you opposite things at the aggregate and split levels, the data is not lying. The picture is what tells you which view to trust. A fork → split. A mediator → don’t.

section: R workshop — see Simpson’s Paradox happen, then resolve it
text:
R workshop — see Simpson’s Paradox happen, then resolve it
In the lecture, we walked Hassan through the trap and back out using a picture. In this workshop you’ll build the exact same dataset in R, watch the paradox appear in your console, and then watch how the choice of picture determines whether you should disaggregate.

Setting up

library(dplyr)
library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)



Build the dataset from the lecture
The numbers are exactly those from the lecture table — 100 voucher households and 100 non-voucher households, split by whether the household lives in an easy-to-reach area (close to a registered facility) or a hard-to-reach area.

voucher_data <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Access,         ~Voucher, ~ClinicDelivery, ~n,
  "easy",          "yes",    "yes",           60,
  "easy",          "yes",    "no",            10,
  "easy",          "no",     "yes",           45,
  "easy",          "no",     "no",            5,
  "hard",          "yes",    "yes",           5,
  "hard",          "yes",    "no",            25,
  "hard",          "no",     "yes",           10,
  "hard",          "no",     "no",            40
) |>
  tidyr::uncount(n)

nrow(voucher_data)  # 200 rows



The aggregate view (what Hassan saw first)

voucher_data |>
  group_by(Voucher) |>
  summarise(
    pct_clinic = mean(ClinicDelivery == "yes")
  )

You’ll see voucher = 65%, no voucher = 55%. A clean +10 percentage points in favour of the voucher.


The split view (what Naomi told Hassan to look at)

voucher_data |>
  group_by(Access, Voucher) |>
  summarise(
    pct_clinic = mean(ClinicDelivery == "yes"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Now look at every Access × Voucher cell:

Easy to reach: voucher 86%, no voucher 90% — voucher slightly worse
Hard to reach: voucher 17%, no voucher 20% — voucher slightly worse

In both access groups, voucher does worse than no voucher. Same data. Opposite story. Simpson’s Paradox is staring at you from your console.


Let the picture decide which view to trust

# Hassan's picture: access is upstream of voucher AND of clinic delivery.
# (The voucher rolled out where existing clinics could redeem it, so the
# programme is concentrated in easier-to-reach areas — and easier-to-reach
# areas have higher clinic delivery for many other reasons too.)
# That makes access a confounder — exactly the fork shape from Chapter 2.
voucher_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Access  -> Voucher
  Access  -> ClinicDelivery
  Voucher -> ClinicDelivery
}')

ggdag(voucher_dag, text_size = 4) + theme_dag()

# Ask the picture: to estimate Voucher -> ClinicDelivery, what do we need to adjust for?
adjustmentSets(voucher_dag,
               exposure = "Voucher",
               outcome  = "ClinicDelivery")

R will tell you: Access. The picture says access is a confounder, so you have to adjust for it — meaning the split view is the right one. The aggregate is misleading.


What if the picture were different?

# Alternative picture: the voucher itself creates effective access (e.g., it
# includes a transport subsidy that pays for the motorbike). In this picture
# Access is downstream of Voucher — a mediator. Adjusting for it would BLOCK
# the very effect you're trying to measure.
mediator_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Voucher -> Access
  Access  -> ClinicDelivery
  Voucher -> ClinicDelivery
}')

adjustmentSets(mediator_dag,
               exposure = "Voucher",
               outcome  = "ClinicDelivery")

R will return an empty set — meaning, in this picture, you should not adjust for access. The aggregate is right, the split is wrong.
Same data. Two pictures. Opposite advice. This is exactly the point from the lecture: the data alone cannot pick a winner. The picture has to.

title: Chapter 4 — Putting Numbers on the Picture
text:
Tanzania’s national maternal mortality ratio is 524 per 100,000 live births (WHO 2017). But Joyce — a midwife in Mwanza Region — does not deliver 100,000 births. She delivers about 100 a year. A number that’s right at the country level can be useless at the bedside. We need a way to take the picture from Chapters 2–3 and turn each arrow into a number Joyce can actually use.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: A picture from Chapter 2 + a lookup table on every arrow = a Bayesian network. The picture tells you the structure; the counts tell you the strengths.

title: Chapter 4 — Putting Numbers on the Picture
section: R workshop — build Joyce’s first Bayesian network
text:
R workshop — build Joyce’s first Bayesian network
In the lecture, we built the smallest possible picture-with-numbers for Joyce’s facility: Anaemia → BadOutcome, with the counts from her last 100 mothers (5 anaemia mothers had a bad outcome, 1 non-anaemia mother had one). In this workshop you’ll do the same in R using the bnlearn package — and then ask the network the same forward and backward questions Joyce asks at the bedside.

Setting up

# bnlearn handles Bayesian networks (pictures with lookup tables on the arrows).
# gRain lets us ask the network specific questions.
library(bnlearn)
library(gRain)



Joyce’s picture, with structure only

# First, just the picture (no numbers yet).
# Two boxes, one arrow — the smallest possible Bayesian network.
joyce_dag <- model2network("[Anaemia][BadOutcome|Anaemia]")

# Show the structure
plot(joyce_dag)

What you should see: two boxes with one arrow. Anaemia → BadOutcome. The same shape as the lecture diagram.


Now add Joyce’s lookup table
The counts come straight from Joyce’s logbook — exactly the table from the lecture.

# Joyce had 40 anaemia mothers and 60 non-anaemia mothers out of 100.
# Think of these as "40 out of 100", not "0.40".
prob_anaemia <- array(
  c(0.40, 0.60),
  dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Anaemia = c("yes", "no"))
)

# Of every 40 anaemia mothers, 5 had a bad outcome (5/40 = 12.5%) and 35 did not.
# Of every 60 non-anaemia mothers, 1 had a bad outcome (1/60 ≈ 1.7%) and 59 did not.
prob_bad_given_anaemia <- array(
  c(0.125, 0.875,    # Anaemia = yes  → bad 5/40 = 12.5%, good 87.5%
    0.0167, 0.9833), # Anaemia = no   → bad 1/60 ≈ 1.7%,  good 98.3%
  dim = c(2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    BadOutcome = c("yes", "no"),
    Anaemia    = c("yes", "no")
  )
)

# Stitch the table onto the picture.
joyce_bn <- custom.fit(joyce_dag, dist = list(
  Anaemia    = prob_anaemia,
  BadOutcome = prob_bad_given_anaemia
))



Ask the network Joyce’s bedside questions
The whole point of the picture-with-numbers is that the same lookup table answers different questions when you ask it from different directions.

# Convert to gRain format so we can run queries.
joyce_grain <- as.grain(joyce_bn)

# FORWARD question: a new mother walks in with anaemia.
# What's the chance of a bad outcome?
querygrain(setEvidence(joyce_grain,
                       evidence = list(Anaemia = "yes")),
           nodes = "BadOutcome")

# BACKWARD question: a bad outcome happened.
# What's the chance the mother had anaemia?
querygrain(setEvidence(joyce_grain,
                       evidence = list(BadOutcome = "yes")),
           nodes = "Anaemia")

What you should see:

Forward question returns about 12.5% — that’s 5 out of 40 anaemia mothers having a bad outcome.
Backward question returns about 83% — that’s 5 of the 6 bad outcomes happening in anaemia mothers.

Same table, two questions, two answers. That is the magic of putting numbers on the picture. The arrow can run in both directions when you ask the network a question.
crumbs: Chapter 4 — Putting Numbers on the Picture

title: Chapter 2 — Drawing the Picture
text:
Rwanda’s neonatal mortality rate fell from 41 to 19 per 1,000 live births between 2000 and 2019 (DHS Rwanda 2000; 2019/20). The front line was about 45,000 community health workers — almost all women, almost all volunteers, with six days of training each (Rwanda Biomedical Centre, 2020).
How can volunteers with six days of training help drive one of the fastest declines on record? The answer is in the picture, not the training.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: A causal diagram is just three node types, signed arrows, and three shapes — and once you know that grammar, you can draw a picture for any programme you encounter.

title: Chapter 2 — Drawing the Picture
section: R workshop — build Beatrice’s diagram, then check the shapes
text:
R workshop — build Beatrice’s diagram, then check the shapes
In the lecture, we built Beatrice’s full picture: a fork at the top (the government CHW programme spawning both her training and the new ambulance route), a chain running through her visits and the mother’s recognition of danger signs, and a collider at the survival outcome. In this workshop you’ll build that diagram in R and ask dagitty to find the chains, forks, and colliders for you — so you don’t have to spot them by eye.

Setting up

# Same two packages as Chapter 1.
library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)



Beatrice’s full picture, in code

# Build the diagram exactly as it appeared in the lecture.
# Read each line as "this one influences that one".
beatrice_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  CHW_Programme   -> Training
  CHW_Programme   -> Ambulance
  Training        -> Visits
  Visits          -> DangerSigns
  DangerSigns     -> NewbornSurvives
  Ambulance       -> NewbornSurvives
  Distance        -> NewbornSurvives
  Distance        -> Visits
  Poverty         -> Visits
  Poverty         -> NewbornSurvives
}')

coordinates(beatrice_dag) <- list(
  x = c(CHW_Programme = 1, Training = 0, Ambulance = 2,
        Visits = 0, DangerSigns = 1, NewbornSurvives = 2,
        Distance = 2, Poverty = -1),
  y = c(CHW_Programme = 3, Training = 2, Ambulance = 2,
        Visits = 1, DangerSigns = 1, NewbornSurvives = 0,
        Distance = 2, Poverty = 1)
)

ggdag(beatrice_dag, text_size = 3) + theme_dag()



Let R find the shapes for you
dagitty knows the grammar from Chapter 2. You can ask it to list the chains, forks, and colliders without spotting them by eye.

# All the paths between the action (Visits) and the outcome.
# dagitty marks each path as 'open' (the influence flows) or 'blocked'.
paths(beatrice_dag, from = "Visits", to = "NewbornSurvives")

What you should see: at least one open path going Visits -> DangerSigns -> NewbornSurvives (that’s the chain), and at least one path involving Poverty (which is a fork — Poverty is the shared parent of Visits and NewbornSurvives).
Now let’s ask the same adjustmentSets question we asked in Chapter 1 — but with a richer picture.

# What do we need to adjust for to estimate Visits -> NewbornSurvives?
adjustmentSets(beatrice_dag,
               exposure = "Visits",
               outcome  = "NewbornSurvives")

R will tell you which variables you’d need to control for. Notice: it does not include DangerSigns, because DangerSigns is on the chain between Visits and the outcome — adjusting for it would block the very path you’re trying to measure. The grammar from the lecture is doing real work here.

title: Chapter 2 — Drawing the Picture
text:
Try it yourself
A new programme will train CHWs in a neighbouring district to use a smartphone app for danger-sign screening. Before you fund it, draw the picture. Where does the smartphone go? Where does phone signal go? Where does literacy go? Where does the mother’s trust in technology go?
In Chapter 3, we’ll turn this exact exercise into a method — building a causal picture by interviewing the people who run the programme.

The textbook this course is adapted from
Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014). Inference and Intervention: Causal Models for Business Analysis. Routledge.
The textbook this course is built on. Ryall and Bramson developed the framework — qualitative pictures, quantitative tables, decision maps, game theory, structure learning — for business decisions. We have adapted every chapter for public health and Maternal & Newborn Health, with new examples drawn entirely from public MNH data.

title: References
text:
Causal inference and decision theory

Pearl, J. & Mackenzie, D. (2018). The Book of Why: The New Science of Cause and Effect. Basic Books. The most readable introduction to causal inference in print.
Pearl, J., Glymour, M. & Jewell, N. (2016). Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer. Wiley. Short, careful, with worked examples.
Hernán, M. A. & Robins, J. M. (2020). Causal Inference: What If. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Open-access at hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book.
Spirtes, P., Glymour, C. & Scheines, R. (2000). Causation, Prediction, and Search (2nd ed.). MIT Press. The foundational text on the PC algorithm and structure learning. Open-access online.
Howard, R. A. & Abbas, A. E. (2015). Foundations of Decision Analysis. Pearson. The textbook on decision trees, expected value, and the value of perfect information.
Dixit, A. & Nalebuff, B. (2008). The Art of Strategy. Norton. The most readable introduction to game theory ever written. No equations.
Gigerenzer, G. (2002). Calculated Risks: How to Know When Numbers Deceive You. Simon & Schuster. The book that convinced an entire generation of doctors to teach probability in natural frequencies.
Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. Journal of Finance, 7(1). The classic finance paper that started portfolio thinking. Twelve pages. Worth reading once.

A note on protagonists
Every named protagonist in this course — Almaz, Beatrice, Faith, Joyce, Hiwot, Hassan, Naomi, David, Grace, Wangari, Patrick, Esther — is a composite. The details (ages, locations, situations, decisions) are drawn from the public sources listed above. The names are not real. Composites are clearly labeled at every introduction. We use this convention to give each chapter an emotional anchor without putting any real person on the spot.

title: Causal Analysis in Public Health Management
text:
Her baby lived. A Health Extension Worker was in the room. So was a new road that had cut the trip to the nearest hospital from four hours to ninety minutes. So was a school year that had kept her in class until she was nineteen.
Which of those things saved her baby?
That question — which of the things happening at the same time actually mattered — is the question this course is about.






Note



A practical course on causal thinking for global health. Designed for high school learners with no statistics or programming background. Built around real Maternal & Newborn Health stories from Ethiopia, Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania, using public data from WHO, UNICEF, DHS, and Lancet.

title: Chapter 1 — Did It Actually Work?
text:
Between 2000 and 2016, maternal mortality in Ethiopia fell from 673 to 412 deaths per 100,000 live births (DHS Ethiopia 2000; 2016).
Over the same period, Ethiopia trained about 38,000 Health Extension Workers (WHO 2013).
But facility delivery rates only rose from 5% in 2005 to 26% in 2016 (DHS Ethiopia 2005; 2016). Most births were still happening at home during the years when mortality was falling fastest.
So what was actually working?






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: Two things happening together is not the same as one causing the other — and figuring out which is which is the whole job of causal analysis.

title: Chapter 1 — Did It Actually Work?
text:
R workshop — draw Almaz’s picture
In the lecture, we drew Almaz’s situation as a small diagram with four boxes — government funding at the top, the Health Extension Worker and the new road as siblings underneath, and the baby’s survival at the bottom. In this workshop you’ll draw that same diagram in R, then ask R one specific question: if I add the road to my picture, does the apparent effect of the HEW change?
You don’t need to install anything yet. Read the code first. Run it later if you want.

Setting up
We use a small package called dagitty for drawing causal diagrams, and ggdag for making them look nice on screen.

# Load the two packages we need.
# dagitty handles the math of causal diagrams.
# ggdag turns them into pictures.
library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)



Almaz’s picture, in code
This is the diagram from the lecture. Each line is one arrow.

# Build the diagram.
# Read each arrow as "this one influences that one".
almaz_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Funding   -> HEW
  Funding   -> Road
  HEW       -> BabySurvives
  Road      -> BabySurvives
}')

# Tell ggdag where to put each box on the page.
coordinates(almaz_dag) <- list(
  x = c(Funding = 1, HEW = 0, Road = 2, BabySurvives = 1),
  y = c(Funding = 2, HEW = 1, Road = 1, BabySurvives = 0)
)

# Draw it.
ggdag(almaz_dag, text_size = 4) + theme_dag()

What you should see: a four-box picture. Funding sits at the top. Two arrows come down from it to the HEW box on the left and the Road box on the right. Then both of those have arrows pointing down to BabySurvives at the bottom.
This picture makes one thing visible that the words alone don’t: the HEW and the road share a parent. They came in the same package. That’s the whole reason it’s hard to tell which one mattered.


The one specific question
Now we ask dagitty the question from the lecture: if we want to estimate the effect of the HEW on whether the baby survives, what else do we need to take into account?

# Ask: to estimate HEW -> BabySurvives, what do we need to control for?
adjustmentSets(almaz_dag,
               exposure  = "HEW",
               outcome   = "BabySurvives")

R will tell you: Road.
That’s the answer. If you want to know whether the HEW actually made a difference, you cannot just look at villages with HEWs versus villages without. You have to compare them at the same level of road access — because the road is doing some of the work, and the HEW is doing some of the work, and right now you can’t tell how much of each.
This is the whole game we’re going to play for the rest of the course: draw the picture, then let the picture tell you which questions are answerable and which ones aren’t.

title: Chapter 1 — Did It Actually Work?
text:
Try it yourself
A neighbouring district to Almaz’s launches a free SMS reminder service for pregnant women in 2018. By 2020, antenatal visit rates in that district have risen by 12 percentage points. The district health officer wants more funding to expand it.
Before you write your funding recommendation, draw the picture. What boxes would you put on it? What arrows? What other thing might have changed in that district between 2018 and 2020 — and where does it go on the picture?
We’ll come back to this exact scenario in Chapter 2.

title: Chapter 3 — Building the Picture from Scratch
text:
Kenya devolved health to 47 counties in 2013 (Constitution of Kenya, Schedule 4). Some counties have cut maternal mortality dramatically. Others have barely moved (Kenya Health Information System, county dashboards). The county dashboards can tell you which counties are improving — but not why.
To find out why, you have to go talk to people. The question is who, in what order, and what to do with what they tell you.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: The fastest way to build a useful causal picture is to interview the people who actually do the work — in three different groups, in a particular order — and draw their answers.

title: Chapter 3 — Building the Picture from Scratch
section: R workshop — assemble Faith’s three interviews
text:
R workshop — assemble Faith’s three interviews
In the lecture, Faith built her picture from three interviews — Mary the midwife, Lokol the husband, Esther the finance officer. Each one added boxes the others couldn’t see. In this workshop you’ll do the same thing in R: start with Mary’s chain, add Lokol’s permission box, add Esther’s stockout box, and watch how the picture grows.

Setting up

library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)



Step 1 — Mary’s picture (the bedside)

mary_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Bleeding -> FamilyWaits
  FamilyWaits -> Motorbike
  Motorbike -> ArrivesAtFacility
  ArrivesAtFacility -> MotherDies
}')
ggdag(mary_dag, text_size = 3) + theme_dag()

A clean chain. Five boxes, four arrows. This is what Mary saw — and only what Mary saw.


Step 2 — Lokol’s correction (the household)
Lokol’s interview reveals that “FamilyWaits” was actually two boxes — the deciding, and the permission from the head of family. Let’s split it.

mary_lokol_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Bleeding -> FamilyDecides
  FamilyDecides -> Permission
  Permission -> Motorbike
  Motorbike -> ArrivesAtFacility
  ArrivesAtFacility -> MotherDies
}')
ggdag(mary_lokol_dag, text_size = 3) + theme_dag()

The chain grew by one box. The new box (Permission) sits where Mary’s “waits” used to be — and it’s the box Mary couldn’t see, because she wasn’t in the household.


Step 3 — Esther’s layer (the supply chain)
Esther’s stockout has nothing to do with the bedside chain — it sits in a different part of the picture entirely, with its own arrow into the death-outcome box.

faith_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  NationalSupplier -> CountyStockout
  CountyStockout -> DrugAtFacility
  DrugAtFacility -> MotherDies

  Bleeding -> FamilyDecides
  FamilyDecides -> Permission
  Permission -> Motorbike
  Motorbike -> ArrivesAtFacility
  ArrivesAtFacility -> MotherDies
}')

coordinates(faith_dag) <- list(
  x = c(NationalSupplier = 0, CountyStockout = 1, DrugAtFacility = 2,
        Bleeding = 0, FamilyDecides = 1, Permission = 2,
        Motorbike = 3, ArrivesAtFacility = 4, MotherDies = 5),
  y = c(NationalSupplier = 2, CountyStockout = 2, DrugAtFacility = 2,
        Bleeding = 0, FamilyDecides = 0, Permission = 0,
        Motorbike = 0, ArrivesAtFacility = 0, MotherDies = 1)
)

ggdag(faith_dag, text_size = 2.5) + theme_dag()

What you should see: two layers feeding into a single death-outcome. The bedside layer at the bottom. The supply-chain layer up top. Joined only at the very end. (We use the death framing because Mary’s interview was specifically about what causes deaths — and the picture should reflect what the source actually said.)


Asking the picture which arrows you’d need to test

# How many distinct paths run from the start of the bleeding chain to the
# death-outcome? Each one is a place a programme could intervene.
paths(faith_dag, from = "Bleeding", to = "MotherDies")

R will show you that there’s only one path — but it has six links in it. Every one of those links is a place a programme could intervene to break the chain and save the life. And the picture tells you that DrugAtFacility is on a completely separate path, controlled by an entirely different set of people.
This is the practical payoff of the interview method: the finished picture makes the intervention points visible.

title: Chapter 5 — When New Evidence Arrives
text:
A regional health director in Amhara opens her email Monday morning. Maternal deaths in one of her districts jumped from 9 to 14 in a single quarter. Three explanations sit on the table within the hour: personnel attrition, a measles surge, or a reporting pipeline cleanup. Over the next two weeks, evidence will arrive piece by piece. Her belief has to update each time — without overreacting.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: Bayesian updating is just redistributing your “out of 100” between explanations — keeping the total at 100 — based on which ones the new evidence fits.

title: Chapter 5 — When New Evidence Arrives
section: R workshop — update Hiwot’s belief as evidence arrives
text:
R workshop — update Hiwot’s belief as evidence arrives
In the lecture, we walked through Hiwot’s three competing explanations, started with a 33-33-33 prior, and watched the numbers move twice — once on Tuesday, once on Wednesday. In this workshop you’ll do the same updating in R, using the same Bayesian network machinery from Chapter 4.

Setting up

library(bnlearn)
library(gRain)



A picture for the three competing explanations

# Three boxes: each is one of Hiwot's three explanations.
# All three feed into the observed rise in deaths.
hiwot_dag <- model2network("[Personnel][Measles][Reporting][DeathsRose|Personnel:Measles:Reporting]")

plot(hiwot_dag)

What you should see: three parents (Personnel, Measles, Reporting) and one child (DeathsRose). Each parent could on its own explain the rise — that’s the collider shape from Chapter 2.


Fill in the lookup tables

# Hiwot's prior: roughly 33-33-33 across the three explanations.
prior_personnel <- c(yes = 0.33, no = 0.67)
prior_measles   <- c(yes = 0.33, no = 0.67)
prior_reporting <- c(yes = 0.33, no = 0.67)

# DeathsRose is "yes" if any of the three parents is "yes" (a noisy-OR).
# IMPORTANT: R fills array() in column-major order — the FIRST dimension
# (DeathsRose) varies fastest, then Personnel, then Measles, then Reporting.
# Each pair below is (P(DeathsRose=yes), P(DeathsRose=no)) for one combination
# of the three parents.
deaths_table <- array(
  c(
    # Reporting = no, Measles = no
    0.05, 0.95,   # Personnel = no   (none of the three: baseline)
    0.70, 0.30,   # Personnel = yes  (personnel only)
    # Reporting = no, Measles = yes
    0.70, 0.30,   # Personnel = no   (measles only)
    0.95, 0.05,   # Personnel = yes  (personnel + measles)
    # Reporting = yes, Measles = no
    0.70, 0.30,   # Personnel = no   (reporting only)
    0.95, 0.05,   # Personnel = yes  (personnel + reporting)
    # Reporting = yes, Measles = yes
    0.95, 0.05,   # Personnel = no   (measles + reporting)
    0.99, 0.01    # Personnel = yes  (all three)
  ),
  dim = c(2, 2, 2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    DeathsRose = c("yes", "no"),
    Personnel  = c("no", "yes"),
    Measles    = c("no", "yes"),
    Reporting  = c("no", "yes")
  )
)

hiwot_bn <- custom.fit(hiwot_dag, dist = list(
  Personnel  = prior_personnel,
  Measles    = prior_measles,
  Reporting  = prior_reporting,
  DeathsRose = deaths_table
))

hiwot_grain <- as.grain(hiwot_bn)



Monday: Hiwot only knows the deaths rose

# Just the observation that deaths rose. No other evidence yet.
querygrain(setEvidence(hiwot_grain, evidence = list(DeathsRose = "yes")),
           nodes = c("Personnel", "Measles", "Reporting"))

You’ll see all three explanations sitting roughly close to one another — the prior plus the simple fact “deaths rose”.


Tuesday: the chief of staff calls
The personnel story gains support; the measles story loses support.

querygrain(setEvidence(hiwot_grain,
                       evidence = list(DeathsRose = "yes",
                                       Measles    = "no")),
           nodes = c("Personnel", "Measles", "Reporting"))

Personnel is now meaningfully more likely than reporting.


Wednesday: the HMIS officer confirms a coding cleanup
This is the explaining away moment from the lecture.

querygrain(setEvidence(hiwot_grain,
                       evidence = list(DeathsRose = "yes",
                                       Measles    = "no",
                                       Reporting  = "yes")),
           nodes = c("Personnel", "Measles", "Reporting"))

Watch what happens to Personnel. Even though no new evidence about personnel arrived, its probability drops — because reporting is now absorbing more of the rise. That’s the redistribution rule from the lecture, doing the work without you.

title: Chapter 5 — When New Evidence Arrives
text:
Try it yourself
A regional director in Kenya sees antenatal coverage in one county jump from 65% to 78% in a single quarter. Three explanations: a new SMS reminder programme, a DHIS2 coding change, or a measles vaccination drive that brought women into clinics where they were also screened for ANC. Start with 33-33-33. A phone call confirms the DHIS2 coding change is real. How do your numbers move? What’s the next piece of evidence you should ask for?

title: Chapter 7 — From Understanding to Deciding
section: R workshop — compute David’s expected value, then his EVPI
text:
R workshop — compute David’s expected value, then his EVPI
In the lecture, David weighed Bahati against Nakuru using natural-frequency expected values. In this workshop you’ll do the same calculation in R, then compute the Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) — the answer to “would more research actually change my decision?”.

Setting up

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)



David’s two options

# Each row is one possible future for one option, with the lives saved and
# the probability of that future.
options <- tribble(
  ~option,        ~scenario,    ~lives_saved, ~prob,
  "Bahati",       "good year",  8,            0.60,
  "Bahati",       "bad year",   2,            0.40,
  "Nakuru town",  "good year",  5,            0.80,
  "Nakuru town",  "bad year",   1,            0.20
)

options



Compute the expected value for each option

options |>
  group_by(option) |>
  summarise(
    expected_lives_saved = sum(lives_saved * prob)
  )

You should see Bahati at 5.6 and Nakuru town at 4.2. Bahati wins by 1.4 lives per year.


Compute the Expected Value of Perfect Information
EVPI requires us to enumerate the joint scenarios across both options, not just one. We assume Bahati’s good/bad year is independent of Nakuru’s good/bad year — a rough but defensible assumption when the two facilities are far enough apart that local shocks (rainfall, road closures, staff turnover) don’t move together.

# Bahati and Nakuru as two separate uncertain sources.
bahati_states <- tibble(state = c("good", "bad"), lives = c(8, 2), prob = c(0.6, 0.4))
nakuru_states <- tibble(state = c("good", "bad"), lives = c(5, 1), prob = c(0.8, 0.2))

# All four joint states (Bahati state x Nakuru state).
joint <- tidyr::crossing(
  b_state = bahati_states$state,
  n_state = nakuru_states$state
) |>
  mutate(
    b_lives = bahati_states$lives[match(b_state, bahati_states$state)],
    n_lives = nakuru_states$lives[match(n_state, nakuru_states$state)],
    b_prob  = bahati_states$prob[match(b_state, bahati_states$state)],
    n_prob  = nakuru_states$prob[match(n_state, nakuru_states$state)],
    joint_prob = b_prob * n_prob,
    # In each joint state, with perfect info you'd pick the option that
    # actually saves more lives in that state.
    best_lives = pmax(b_lives, n_lives)
  )

joint

# EV under uncertainty: David picks the single option with the highest
# expected value (Bahati at 5.6) and lives with whatever year actually happens.
ev_no_info <- max(
  sum(bahati_states$lives * bahati_states$prob),
  sum(nakuru_states$lives * nakuru_states$prob)
)
ev_no_info

# EV with perfect information: in each joint state, David picks the best
# option for that state.
ev_with_info <- sum(joint$best_lives * joint$joint_prob)
ev_with_info

# EVPI = how much you'd gain on average from knowing the future before deciding.
evpi <- ev_with_info - ev_no_info
evpi

What you should see: ev_no_info is 5.6 (Bahati’s expected value), ev_with_info is around 6.56, and evpi is around 0.96 — about 1 extra life per year. That tells David a perfectly informative one-month study could, in expectation, save him about one extra newborn life — which is meaningful but not enormous. He’d weigh that against the cost of waiting a month before placing the midwife.
This is the “would more research change my decision?” question, made into a number.

text:
Try it yourself
A donor offers your county a free newborn resuscitation device. Two hospitals want it. Hospital A is large and busy with reliable electricity (3 lives saved, high confidence). Hospital B is smaller and rural, with power cuts about half the time (6 lives saved when power holds, 1 when it doesn’t). Compute the expected value for each. Where does the device go?

title: Chapter 9 — When the Other Side Reacts
text:
A donor offers two Kenyan counties the same matching grant for maternal health. Wangari accepts enthusiastically and doubles her maternal health budget. Patrick quietly redirects his maternal health funds to road repairs, knowing the donor will fund maternal health anyway. Same deal. Opposite responses. The donor’s expected-value forecast was wrong in one of the two counties — and the reason it was wrong is the most important lesson in Part 3.






Note



The one thing to remember from this chapter: Your decisions change how other people behave — and unless you write that down, your forecast of impact will be wrong.

section: R workshop — find the Nash equilibrium of the matching grant
text:
R workshop — find the Nash equilibrium of the matching grant
In the lecture, we walked through the four-cell payoff matrix for the matching grant and found by hand that the only stable cell was the worst one. In this workshop you’ll build the matrix in R, ask it for the Nash equilibrium directly, then change one number and watch the equilibrium shift.

Setting up

library(dplyr)



Build the payoff matrix

# We'll represent the game as a small data frame.
# Each row is one cell of the matrix. Payoffs are in arbitrary units —
# higher = better for that player.
game <- tibble::tribble(
  ~county_action,    ~donor_action,    ~county_payoff, ~donor_payoff,
  "fund",            "match",          5,              5,
  "fund",            "walk_away",      2,              0,
  "redirect",        "match",          7,              -2,
  "redirect",        "walk_away",      4,              0
)

game

The payoffs reflect the lecture’s reasoning:

fund + match is good for both — but the county is leaving roads unrepaired.
redirect + match is best for the county (gets roads + match) but worst for the donor (money wasted).
redirect + walk_away is the cautious outcome — county gets roads, donor saves face.



Find the Nash equilibrium by hand
A cell is a Nash equilibrium if neither player would improve by switching unilaterally.

find_nash <- function(g) {
  g |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(
      # Best response by the COUNTY, holding the donor's choice fixed
      county_best = max(g$county_payoff[g$donor_action == donor_action]),
      county_at_best = (county_payoff == county_best),

      # Best response by the DONOR, holding the county's choice fixed
      donor_best = max(g$donor_payoff[g$county_action == county_action]),
      donor_at_best = (donor_payoff == donor_best),

      is_nash = county_at_best & donor_at_best
    ) |>
    ungroup()
}

find_nash(game) |>
  select(county_action, donor_action, county_payoff, donor_payoff, is_nash)

You should see exactly one row with is_nash = TRUE — the bottom-right cell, where the county redirects and the donor walks away. The rational equilibrium is the worst outcome for everyone. That’s the lecture’s point in numbers.


Now fix the game with conditionality
Suppose the donor adds a clause: “the match only triggers if total maternal health spending rises by at least X.” This penalises redirect + match for the county — the county can no longer game the system to get both the match and the road repairs.

game_fixed <- game |>
  mutate(county_payoff = case_when(
    county_action == "redirect" & donor_action == "match" ~ -1,  # large penalty
    TRUE ~ county_payoff
  ))

find_nash(game_fixed) |>
  select(county_action, donor_action, county_payoff, donor_payoff, is_nash)

Look carefully at the output. You should now see TWO rows with is_nash = TRUE — both fund + match AND the original redirect + walk_away.
That is not a bug. Conditionality didn’t eliminate the bad equilibrium; it created a viable alternative good one. We now have two stable cells, and the question becomes: which one will the players actually coordinate on?
This is where the language of the contract starts to matter. The conditionality clause acts as a focal point — a shared, public expectation that picks one of the two equilibria. Both players know the donor will enforce the clause, both know the county now has nothing to gain from gaming it, and both coordinate on the cooperative cell. The clause’s job is not to make the bad outcome impossible (it can’t); its job is to make the cooperative outcome the obvious place to settle.
Game theory rarely produces a single answer. It produces a small set of stable answers, and the language of the contract picks among them. That is the whole purpose of grant design — not to compel cooperation, but to make cooperation focal.
